questions.prompt: How does enterprise triage invert the single-host collection strategy?
options: It images every endpoint in parallel
It collects a small targeted artifact set from many hosts, rather than everything from one, to decide which few warrant deep analysis
It relies entirely on EDR alerts
It collects nothing until a host is confirmed compromised
questions.explanation: The question shifts from 'what happened here' to 'which machines does this apply to', which requires kilobytes per host rather than full disk images.

questions.prompt: What is frequency analysis (stacking), and why does it work without signatures?
options: Counting how often an alert fires per day
Aggregating one artifact type across the fleet, sorting by count, and examining the rarest values -- a service on 3 machines out of 4,000 is an outlier regardless of whether anyone has seen it before
questions.explanation: Because a healthy estate is overwhelmingly homogeneous, rarity itself becomes the signal -- which is precisely where signature-based detection fails.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Kansa's role from KAPE's?
options: KAPE is targeted per-host collection; Kansa is a PowerShell Remoting framework for fleet-wide sweeps that also ships frequency-analysis scripts for stacking results
KAPE performs remote sweeps and Kansa does local collection
questions.explanation: Kansa's real strength is the analysis half -- stacking results across the estate to surface outliers, not just gathering them.

questions.prompt: Why is collection that sprays local admin credentials across the estate a red flag?
options: It is too slow to be practical
It recreates the credential-exposure problem that enables pass-the-hash lateral movement
It violates GDPR in all jurisdictions
questions.explanation: Distributing privileged credentials to every endpoint to enable collection creates exactly the harvestable-credential condition attackers rely on.
